title: ACA s. 29A — Time limit for arbitral award (ACA s. 29A)

content.overview: Section 29A regulates the time for making an arbitral award. For arbitrations other than international commercial arbitration, the statutory period runs from completion of pleadings under section 23(4). The parties may extend the period by consent for the statutory additional period, and the Court may grant further extension on application under the conditions and consequences specified by the Act. The section also regulates fees and substitution in appropriate cases.

content.study:
Statutory commencement point: The period is tied to completion of pleadings under section 23(4) for the arbitrations covered by the statutory period.

Consent extension: The parties may extend the statutory period by the additional period permitted by the Act.

Judicial extension: The Court may extend the time on application under section 29A and may impose the statutory consequences concerning fees and substitution.

Substitution and continuation: Where substitution is ordered, the Act governs continuation and the statutory treatment of the reconstituted tribunal.

examples.title: Calculation
examples.body: Counsel first establishes the completion date of pleadings, then calculates the statutory period and any valid extension.

examples.title: Court extension
examples.body: If the statutory period is insufficient, the party seeks the judicial extension contemplated by section 29A before relying on an informal enlargement.

hypotheticals.question: From what event is the statutory period calculated?
hypotheticals.analysis: For the arbitrations covered by the principal time-limit in section 29A, identify completion of pleadings under section 23(4). Then calculate the statutory period and any valid extension.

hypotheticals.question: Can parties simply ignore the statutory time limit?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. The Act specifies the consent extension and judicial extension mechanisms and their consequences.

misconceptions.trap: The time limit runs automatically from the first hearing.
misconceptions.correction: The statutory calculation is tied to completion of pleadings under section 23(4) for the relevant arbitration.

misconceptions.trap: Any informal agreement automatically overrides section 29A.
misconceptions.correction: Use only the extension mechanisms recognised by the Act.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should section 29A be calculated?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify completion of pleadings under section 23(4), calculate the statutory period, identify any valid consent extension, and if necessary invoke the judicial extension mechanism under section 29A.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Time computation must be tied to the statutory trigger.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should a section 29A application establish?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: The pleadings-completion date, expiry calculation, any consent extension, the need for further time and the statutory consequences sought or opposed.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should ACA section 29a be applied?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Identify the statutory trigger, conditions, exceptions and consequence and apply them to the facts.

examTips: Identify the statutory trigger before calculating time.
Separate consent extension from judicial extension.
Address fee and substitution consequences expressly.
